Please review the following manuscript. I've poured years of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b04/review-experiment-ylouw7z2/call-a6dc5e96320a437eb1a3e402d695dc9a/manuscript.pdf

ls -l manuscript.pdf
command -v pdftotext

command -v pdfinfo
command -v python3'

import importlib.util
for m in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
 print(m,importlib.util.find_spec(m))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs
python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 t=p.extract_text()
 parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
for i in range(1,13):
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.png').unlink()
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').unlink()
Path('tmp/pdfs').rmdir()
Path('tmp').rmdir()
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP: repeated stimuli and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate estimates of generalization to unseen language.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is a sensible protocol for evaluating unseen-text decoding from unseen people. The graph formulation and diagrams communicate the intended constraints effectively.
The experiments cover both fMRI and EEG, two established model frameworks, and four seeds for the overlap analysis. The manuscript also acknowledges that its protocol discards data.
weaknesses: The central claim conflates different evaluation targets with data leakage. Different recordings from the same subject can legitimately support within-subject evaluation; shared stimuli can support cross-subject evaluation on known stimuli. Neither establishes simultaneous subject-and-text generalization, but neither is intrinsically invalid. The paper should distinguish repeated observations from restrictions imposed by its chosen generalization target and qualify its claim that all existing strategies leak.

Appendix B's pseudocode does not enforce the proposed criterion as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, excludes held-out subjects but permits adding held-out texts to training. Algorithm 2, line 33, excludes held-out tasks but permits adding held-out subjects. Thus, the expansion steps can recreate the overlap they should eliminate. Corrected pseudocode and verifiable split assignments are necessary to substantiate the zero-leakage results.

The leakage metrics are not operationally consistent with their definitions. Equation (8) uses an exact train–test signal intersection, whereas the conceptual definition concerns shared subjects. Disjoint EEG observations from a shared subject would not explain the reported nonzero rates under this formula. Fully held-out subjects also produce zero denominators without a specified convention. These issues undermine reproducibility of Table 1.

Several reported ROUGE values require correction or explanation. Table 4 gives EEG2Text F1 = 25.74 with recall = 23.98 and precision = 23.95. F1 cannot exceed both under standard consistent aggregation, including ordinary macro averaging. Table 3 contains similar violations. This directly reduces confidence in the benchmark results.

Section 5.2 does not establish the claimed causal effects of leakage. Falling validation loss or improving test scores with additional training does not itself demonstrate overfitting. Table 2 simultaneously changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration, while split comparisons also change data composition and potentially training size. Controlled comparisons are needed to distinguish memorization from optimization effects and increased task difficulty.

Claims that the language decoder dominates and the encoder contributes little lack direct controls, such as shuffled-signal or language-only baselines. The evaluation procedure also does not clearly specify whether reference tokens are supplied during decoding. These omissions leave the interpretation of the generation scores and encoder-contribution claims unresolved.

The proposed benchmark lacks linked code or split artifacts, exact retained subject/story/sample counts, discarded-data fractions, and variability across decoding runs. The four-seed analysis concerns overlap only, which is insufficient to establish decoding robustness with just 12 ZuCo subjects. No quantitative retention comparison supports the data-utilization claim. Together with the algorithm and metric inconsistencies, these soundness and reproducibility gaps warrant revision and resubmission next cycle.
